What the Lake County Recorder does

Land records in Lake County are kept by the Recorder: deeds, mortgages, liens, releases, leases and subdivision plats. The office also takes articles of incorporation, assumed business names, military discharges and UCC filings.

It generally does not handle court orders, decrees, judgments, wills, marriage licenses or birth and death certificates. If the house you are selling came through an estate, the court file and the recorded deed are kept in different places, so expect to visit both. Records can be viewed or purchased at lcrecorder.com, and staff speak Spanish and use sign language.

Office location, hours and phone

Go to Building A, second floor, 2293 N. Main Street, Crown Point, IN 46307. The counter is open weekdays from 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. The phone is 219-755-3730, the fax is (219) 648-6028, and online records live at lcrecorder.com.

Fee schedules and e-recording details are linked from the county's Recorder page. One office serves all 19 incorporated cities and towns across 626.5 square miles, from Gary and Hammond to Crown Point.

From signing to a recorded deed

Sellers rarely visit the Recorder. Still, knowing the sequence helps you spot where a sale can stall.

  1. The deed is prepared with the preparer statement and the Social Security redaction statement.
  2. You and the buyer sign the deed and the sales disclosure form, normally at the title company.
  3. The title company pays off taxes, liens and mortgages from your proceeds and gets releases ready.
  4. The deed and releases go to the Recorder, usually by e-recording through one of the approved vendors, and come back in hours.
  5. The sales disclosure form goes to the assessor for review and then through the Auditor.

If something is rejected, the fix is usually small, such as a missing statement or a wrong parcel number. A corrected document can be resubmitted within hours when it goes in electronically. Paper filings at the second floor counter take longer, so ask your title company which route it uses.

Bring a photo of any older paperwork you have, such as a prior deed, a mortgage release letter or a payoff statement. The Recorder keeps these records, but having your own copy lets the title company check the legal description before closing instead of after.

State recording fees

The recorder's fees come from Indiana Code 36-2-7-10. A deed or any instrument other than a mortgage is $25 to record, and a mortgage is $55.

ServiceFee under IC 36-2-7-10
Deed or other instrument (not a mortgage)$25
Mortgage$55
Page larger than 8.5 by 14 inches$25 for the first page, $5 for each additional
Each added transaction on a release, partial release or assignment$7 on top of the $25 fee
Copy up to 11 by 17 inches$1 per page
Copy larger than 11 by 17 inches$5 per page
Acknowledging or certifying a document$5

Counties may add some charges by ordinance, such as an affordable housing fee of up to $10 per document. Ask the office or your title company for the exact total before closing.

One more fee matters on tax-related releases. For a release of a political subdivision's lien on property sold or transferred under the tax sale and redevelopment statutes, the statute sets $25 per parcel for each subdivision with a lien.

Online access and e-recording fees

A Lake County ordinance sets a few charges tied to the Recorder. Searching the Recorder's website costs $3 per request, with $1 going to the vendor and $2 to the Recorder's Enhanced Access Fund. Printed pages from requested documents cost $1 each, and e-recording carries a $3 charge. Credit card charges vary by card company. Ordinances change, so ask the Recorder to confirm current amounts.

How e-recording works

Lake County has accepted electronic recordings since March 2021 and now receives over half of its documents that way. E-recording is open to title companies, law firms, banks and other businesses that regularly record land records. Documents come back in hours instead of days, and a rejected document can be fixed and resubmitted within hours. Four vendors are approved:

  • Simplifile, which handles both transfer and non-transfer documents (1-800-460-5657)
  • Corporation Service Company, for non-transfer documents (1-866-652-0111)
  • Indecomm Global Services, for non-transfer documents (877-272-5250)
  • GOePN (888-325-3365, ext. 1)

A seller does not sign up for any of these. The title company or closing attorney does it.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Lake County houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

What a deed must show to be recorded

Two statements must appear on the document. One names whoever prepared it, legibly printed, typed, stamped or signed, in a line like "This instrument was prepared by" and a name. The other says the preparer took reasonable care to redact Social Security numbers, under penalty of perjury.

Ahead of the County Auditor, the parties fill out a sales disclosure form and every party signs. The county assessor reviews it first. After the Auditor processes it, it goes back to the assessor, who files it for five years. Plan on one form per parcel.

Covered transfers are deeds and sale contracts for value, plus foreclosure, divorce, court order and probate. Left out are security instruments like mortgages, short-term leases, utility easements and most quitclaim deeds. Questions about the Lake County Auditor's real estate desk go to 219-755-3157.

Closing costs and transfer questions

Recording a deed brings recording and copy charges, as listed above. For a total closing figure, call the Auditor at 219-755-3157 or the Recorder at 219-755-3730, or ask the title company for its settlement statement.

Delinquent taxes and a sale

Back property tax is a claim on the parcel, and a title search finds it before any deed gets recorded. Lake County holds its tax sale online every year, and redemption on certificates from the latest sale runs out September 8, 2027.

A cash buyer deals with these the way a title company does: back taxes, liens and open mortgages come out of the proceeds, releases are recorded, and then the deed. The released liens are separate recordings with their own fees.

  • Collect your deed, tax bill and any payoff letters for liens or mortgages
  • Check the legal description and parcel number against each document
  • At the title company, sign the deed and the sales disclosure form
  • The title company records the deed and releases, through a vendor or at the Recorder
You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

Older properties and title work

Estates, tax sales and long vacancies can leave a house with old liens or releases that were never recorded. Have the title company trace the chain of title early, so a missing release can be recorded before closing.

Frequently asked questions

Where do I record a deed in Lake County, Indiana?

Deeds are recorded with the Lake County Recorder at 2293 N. Main Street, Building A, 2nd Floor in Crown Point. Title companies usually send them electronically.

How much does the Lake County Recorder charge to record a deed?

Indiana Code lists $25 to record a deed or other instrument, and $55 for a mortgage. The county may add charges by ordinance, so ask the office for the current total.

Can I e-record in Lake County?

Yes, through approved vendors, but the service is open to businesses that regularly record land records, such as title companies and banks. Individuals normally use their closing agent.

What is a sales disclosure form in Indiana?

It is a form that every party to a covered conveyance signs before the deed is filed with the county auditor. The assessor reviews it first.

Who do I call at the Lake County Recorder?

Call 219-755-3730 on weekdays between 8:30 a.m. and 4:30 p.m. The fax number is (219) 648-6028.

Marion County, IN County Recorder: Recording a Deed, Fees and Transfer Tax

  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Marion County, IN County Recorder sale

Selling in Marion County? Get a Cash Offer

We buy Marion County houses as-is and reply with a written cash offer.

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

Selling in Marion County?
We buy Marion County houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.

Recorder's Office location, hours and contact

The Marion County Recorder's Office is in the City-County Building, 200 E. Washington Street, Suite T-741, Indianapolis, IN 46204. The counter is open 8 a.m. to 4 p.m., Monday to Friday. The main number is 317.327.4020.

Phones are answered from 9 a.m. to 4 p.m. daily, and a voicemail gets a callback within one to two business days. Email to recorder@indy.gov brings the fastest reply, so use it when your question can wait for a written answer.

This office is the permanent home of the county's property records: deeds, liens, mortgages, easements and survey maps, more than 11 million records in all. Since September 29, 2026 it no longer hands out forms or documents for recording. The reason given is protecting owners from property fraud, so a deed has to come from an attorney, a title company or your own preparation, not from the counter.

How to record a deed

The Assessor stamps the deed before the Recorder sees it. Follow the order on the county's Record Your Deed page, because an unstamped deed cannot be recorded.

  1. Collect the exact name of the current owner and the legal description. The Assessor's property report card or the current tax bill has both.
  2. Prepare the deed. The grantor is the person now on title, and the grantee is the person who will be listed as the new owner. An attorney is the county's recommendation.
  3. Sign it in front of a notary.
  4. Take or mail it to the Assessor for the transfer stamp, with a separate check or money order for each office.
  5. The Recorder records the deed and sends it back to you.
  6. Apply through the Marion County Auditor for any deductions you qualify for.

You can submit by mail, through an e-recording partner or in person. Electronic filing dominates: in November 2025 the office recorded 8,764 documents and 7,948 of them were e-recordings.

Recording fees

Two offices, two sets of fees, two separate payments. The Recorder takes $35.00 per document. The Assessor adds $10.00 per parcel per document for the transfer and $20.00 for each sales disclosure form.

ChargeAmountOffice
Recording fee for a deed$35.00 per documentRecorder
Transfer fee$10.00 per parcel per documentAssessor
Sales disclosure form$20.00 per form, if requiredAssessor
Copies of recorded documents$1 per page up to 11 by 17 inchesRecorder

State law, Indiana Code 36-2-7-10, sets a base fee of $25 for a deed and $55 for a mortgage. A county with a consolidated city can add an optional housing trust fee of $2.50 for the first page and $1 for each added page, an identification security fee of $2, and an optional affordable housing fee of up to $10. Plan around the county's published $35 and let the Recorder's fee schedule decide the total when your document runs long or has unusual features.

Oversized pages cost more: $25 for the first and $5 for each additional. Military discharge papers are recorded free.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Marion County house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

What a deed must include

A deed with a missing statement or a formatting error gets turned away. Each requirement below comes with an Indiana Code citation on the county's requirements page:

  • Notarization (IC 32-21-2-3).
  • A statement under penalties of perjury that reasonable care was taken to redact Social Security numbers, plus the name of the person who prepared the instrument (IC 36-2-11-15).
  • Names of signers and witnesses printed identically throughout and typed under each signature (IC 36-2-11-16).
  • Two-inch top and bottom margins on the first and last pages for the recording stamp. Skip them and an extra page is added (IC 36-2-11-16.5).
  • A street address where tax statements should be mailed (IC 32-21-2-3).
  • For a power of attorney signing, the document number of the power of attorney next to the signature.

The notary's name has to match the commission and appear with the county of residence, the commission expiration date and the date of notarization. Seals on commissions issued or renewed after July 1, 2018 must also carry the words "notary public," "State of Indiana," "seal," and the seven-digit commission number.

To re-record a document you pay the original fee again and state the reason at the top of the page. Include a self-addressed stamped envelope with any paper return.

Transfer fees and the sales disclosure form

Marion County charges flat transfer fees at the Assessor, not a percentage transfer tax: $10 per parcel and $20 per sales disclosure form.

Indiana Code 6-1.1-5.5-3 requires the parties to complete and sign a sales disclosure form before a conveyance document is filed with the county auditor. The Assessor checks the form for accuracy and completeness, approves it and returns it to a party for filing. The county asks you to prepare the form in the Properly system at forms.properlytaxes.com, then print and sign it.

Room W121 is where the paperwork goes. The counter stops processing at 4 p.m. and accepts cash, a check for the exact amount or a card, with a small surcharge on cards. Staff cannot help prepare a deed, so arrive with one an attorney or title company drew up.

Property Fraud Alert

The Recorder promotes a free Property Fraud Alert service for Marion County residents. Sign up at propertyfraudalert.com/INMARION. It is meant to flag activity on your parcel early, before a forged filing causes damage.

An inherited house or one that sits empty is the sort of property worth signing up. The same fraud concern led the office to stop supplying blank recording forms.

The Recorder also offers a survivorship affidavit to remove a deceased owner from title, copies of deeds, a claim form for a recording fee refund and online search of real estate records.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Marion County houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

What goes wrong at closing

The title or escrow company normally arranges the stamp and the recording, so most sellers never touch the process. Knowing it helps you recognize what slows a closing:

  • A missing notary detail, or a name that differs from the vested deed.
  • A legal description that differs from the county's records.
  • A deed submitted without the Assessor stamp.
  • An unreleased mortgage or lien that still appears in the Recorder's index.

On an older house the title can run back through many owners. Ask the title company to review the chain early and flag gaps before a closing date is set. If you are weighing a quick sale of a house with title questions, a written cash offer lets you read the terms and the closing timeline before you commit to anything.

Selling for cash removes the lender's appraisal. The Assessor stamp, the sales disclosure and the recording fee all remain. When you read the contract, find out who pays each charge and get the answer in writing.

Frequently asked questions

How much does it cost to record a deed in Marion County?

The Recorder charges $35.00 per document. The Assessor charges separately: $10.00 per parcel per document, and $20.00 for each sales disclosure when one is required.

Do I record a deed before or after the Assessor stamps it?

After. The Assessor's transfer stamp comes first, and then you take the stamped deed to the Recorder in Room T-741.

Can I e-record a deed in Marion County?

Yes. The office accepts documents by mail, through e-recording partners or in person, and most of what it records now arrives electronically.

Does the Marion County Recorder hand out deed forms?

No. Since September 29, 2026 the office no longer provides forms or documents for recording, so have an attorney or title company draft the deed.

Is there a percentage transfer tax in Marion County?

No. The county lists flat fees: $10 per parcel for the transfer and $20 per sales disclosure at the Assessor, plus the Recorder's fee. Your title company can confirm the total for your sale.

Allen County, IN County Recorder: Recording a Deed, Fees and Transfer Tax

Cash Home Buyers in Indiana
Cash Offer in 24 Hours
  • Allen County, IN County Recorder: inherited, behind on payments, tenants or repairs, we buy the house as-is
  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Allen County, IN County Recorder sale
  • Turn the Allen County, IN County Recorder offer down and you owe us nothing

Selling in Allen County? Get a Cash Offer

We buy Allen County houses as-is and reply with a written cash offer.

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

Selling in Allen County?
We buy Allen County houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.

What the Allen County Recorder does

The recorder keeps the official public record of deeds and mortgages for Allen County, Indiana. When a house sells, the deed is recorded there so the new owner's title is on the public record. The recorder is a separately elected county officer, and the office sits in Fort Wayne, the county seat.

The county treasurer is a different office. It is in the Rousseau Centre at 1 E Main St, Suite 104. Property tax questions go there, while deed and mortgage filings go to the recorder, so call the right office before you make the trip. Your title company usually submits the deed for you, but you should know where the record ends up and who to contact if a recorded document has an error.

Cost to record a deed

Indiana sets the base fee for recording a deed at $25, and a mortgage at $55. Those amounts come from Indiana Code 36-2-7-10, which applies to every county recorder.

Indiana statutory recording fees
Document or serviceFee
Deed or other instrument (not a mortgage)$25
Mortgage$55
Oversized page (larger than 8.5 by 14 inches), first page$25
Oversized page, each additional page$5
Each added transaction on a release, partial release or assignment$7
Copy up to 11 by 17 inches$1 per page
Acknowledging or certifying a document$5
Releasing a political subdivision lien after a tax sale$25 per parcel

A county with an affordable housing fund may add a $10 per document fee by ordinance. Call the recorder to confirm current amounts before you send a check.

What a deed must contain

An Indiana deed needs a preparer statement, an acknowledgment and a Social Security number affirmation. Check each item against your draft before it goes to the recorder.

  • The preparer must be identified on any instrument that needs a preparer statement.
  • The document must include an affirmation, under penalty of perjury, that reasonable care was taken to redact Social Security numbers unless the law requires them.
  • The affirmation goes at the end of the instrument, immediately before or after the preparer statement.
  • A grantee's mailing address that is not a street or rural route address needs a street or rural route address after it. A PO box does not meet the rule.
  • Each signer's name should be typed or printed under the signature exactly as signed.
  • A notarized document should show the notary's county of residence and commission expiration date.

A deed that misses one of these can be turned away, which delays closing. Ask the title company or attorney who prepares the deed to confirm all six before signing day.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Allen County house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

The sales disclosure form

The sales disclosure form goes to the county assessor first and to the county auditor second, and both steps come before the deed is filed. Indiana Code 6-1.1-5.5-3 requires all parties to the conveyance to submit it, including exempt sellers and exempt buyers.

The assessor checks the form for accuracy and completeness. If it passes, the assessor stamps or approves it and returns it to one of the parties, who files it with the auditor.

The rule covers more than ordinary sales. A conveyance document includes transfers made through foreclosure, divorce, court order, condemnation and probate, along with partition documents. It excludes mortgages, trust deeds, leases shorter than 90 years and conveyances to the state or other governments, under IC 6-1.1-5.5-2.

Order of steps for a sale

The deed is signed and notarized first, the sales disclosure form is approved next, and the recorder files the deed last. A typical sequence:

  1. The seller signs the deed in front of a notary, with the preparer statement and Social Security affirmation included.
  2. All parties sign the sales disclosure form.
  3. The county assessor reviews and stamps the form.
  4. The form and deed go to the county auditor.
  5. The recorder records the deed and charges the statutory fee.

When an inherited house is involved, the probate court order and the personal representative's deed have to line up with the names on the title. Check the existing record at the recorder before you list the house.

Checking old records

The Allen County Genealogical Society publishes a free name index of deeds filed with the recorder, covering 1824 to 1903 and 1913 to 1999. If you inherited an older Fort Wayne house and need to understand an old transfer, that index can point you to the right deed.

The index is a finding aid. It does not replace a title search, so ask a title company to run one before you list.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Allen County houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Common problems for sellers

Look for these items before you list. A release that covers several transactions costs an extra $7 for each transaction after the first.

  • A deed prepared with the wrong legal description or a misspelled name.
  • An inherited house where the title still shows a deceased owner.
  • A prior tax sale lien that has to be released, which carries a $25 fee per parcel.
  • A missing sales disclosure approval at the assessor or auditor.

Most of these can be fixed, but each one adds days. A title problem found at the recorder before you list costs far less time than one found two days before closing. If the house needs repairs or the title needs cleanup, a cash buyer who takes properties as-is can work around the condition, though the paperwork above still has to be right for the deed to record.

A sensible routine is to pull the current deed, confirm the names match your ID, check for any open mortgage that was never released, and ask the title company whether any tax sale lien is on the parcel. Bring that short list to your first call with a buyer or agent.

Timing also matters. Recording happens after the sale paperwork is complete, so the deed, the sales disclosure form and the recorder's fee should all be in hand before the closing table. If the title company handles recording, ask when the recorded deed will come back and who pays the fee, so nothing is left unclear after you have the proceeds.

For an inherited house, start with the court order and the personal representative's deed, then compare the names to the record at the recorder. A mismatch, such as a middle initial or a prior owner who never appeared on a recorded deed, is the usual reason a closing slips. Fixing it early means one deed to record instead of a chain of corrective filings. Keep copies of every recorded paper with your closing file, because a later buyer's title search will pull the same record.

Frequently asked questions

How much does it cost to record a deed in Allen County, Indiana?

The statutory fee is $25 for a deed or other non-mortgage instrument and $55 for a mortgage, under Indiana Code 36-2-7-10. Oversized pages and extra transactions cost more. Confirm current amounts with the recorder.

What does an Indiana deed need besides signatures?

It needs an acknowledgment, a preparer statement and an affirmation that reasonable care was taken to redact Social Security numbers. The grantee address must be a street or rural route address rather than a PO box, and a notary should list a county of residence and commission expiration.

What is the sales disclosure form in Indiana?

It is a form signed by all parties to a conveyance. The county assessor reviews and stamps it, and a party then files it with the county auditor before the deed is filed.

Where does the Allen County Treasurer sit?

The treasurer is in the Rousseau Centre at 1 E Main St, Suite 104, Fort Wayne. The recorder is a separate office.

Can I sell an inherited Allen County house without recording anything first?

The deed that transfers the house has to be recorded after the sale, and any prior transfer that left the title in a deceased owner's name may need to be put in order first. A title company can sort that out with you.
